<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>256 Spheres Grid (Three.js)</title>
  <style>
    body { margin: 0; overflow: hidden; }
    canvas { display: block; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <script src="[https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.132.2/build/three.min.js"></script>](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.132.2/build/three.min.js"></script>)
  <script src="[https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.132.2/examples/js/controls/OrbitControls.js"></script>](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.132.2/examples/js/controls/OrbitControls.js"></script>)
  <script>
    // Scene setup
    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(75, window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight, 0.1, 1000);
    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas: document.body.appendChild(document.createElement('canvas')) });
    renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight);
    document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
    // Controls for camera movement
    const controls = new THREE.OrbitControls(camera, renderer.domElement);
    camera.position.z = 20;
    // Create 256 spheres in a 16x16 grid
    const gridSize = 16; // 16x16 = 256
    const sphereRadius = 0.5;
    const spacing = 3.0; // Distance between spheres
    for (let row = 0; row < gridSize; row++) {
      for (let col = 0; col < gridSize; col++) {
        // Calculate position (x, y, z)
        const x = (col - gridSize / 2) * spacing;
        const y = (row - gridSize / 2) * spacing;
        const z = 0;
        // Create a sphere
        const geometry = new THREE.SphereGeometry(sphereRadius, 32, 32);
        const material = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({
          color: Math.random() * 0xffffff, // Random color
          roughness: 0.3,
          metalness: 0.5
        });
        const sphere = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
        sphere.position.set(x, y, z);
        scene.add(sphere);
      }
    }
    // Add lights
    const ambientLight = new THREE.AmbientLight(0xffffff, 0.5);
    scene.add(ambientLight);
    const directionalLight = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 0.8);
    directionalLight.position.set(10, 10, 5);
    scene.add(directionalLight);
    // Animation loop
    function animate() {
      requestAnimationFrame(animate);
      controls.update();
      renderer.render(scene, camera);
    }
    animate();
    // Handle window resize
    window.addEventListener('resize', () => {
      camera.aspect = window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight;
      camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
      renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight);
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>

To build a **Payroll Python Application** for your **Universal Regenerative Universal Basic Income (RUHBI)** concept, we’ll need a structured approach that integrates financial processing, user management, and regenerative economic principles. Below is a **step-by-step breakdown** of how we can design this system, including key components, Python libraries, and automation workflows.

* * *

### **1. Core Features of the RUHBI Payroll System**

Your **RUHBI** concept likely involves:

*   **Universal Basic Income (UBI) distribution** (periodic, unconditional payments).
    
*   **Regenerative economic incentives** (e.g., rewards for sustainable/regenerative activities).
    
*   **Transparent financial tracking** (blockchain-like ledger for trust).
    
*   **Automated compliance** (taxes, social contributions, environmental impact reporting).
    
*   **User self-service portal** (claims, payouts, impact tracking).
    

* * *

### **2. System Architecture**

We’ll use:

*   **Backend**: Python (Flask/FastAPI) for REST APIs.
    
*   **Database**: PostgreSQL (for relational data) + optional IPFS/Blockchain (for transparency).
    
*   **Automation**: Scheduled tasks (Celery) for payouts/tax deductions.
    
*   **Frontend**: Optional (React/Dash for dashboards) or CLI/API-based.
    
*   **Regenerative Tracking**: Integrate with environmental APIs (e.g., carbon footprint calculators).
    

* * *

### **3. Python Libraries & Tools**

| **Component** | **Libraries/Tools** |
| --- | --- |
| **Backend Framework** | Flask, FastAPI, Django |
| **Database** | PostgreSQL (with `psycopg2` or SQLAlchemy) |
| **Authentication** | JWT (PyJWT), OAuth2 |
| **Scheduling** | Celery + Redis/PostgreSQL |
| **Payments** | Stripe, PyCryptodome (for crypto wallets) |
| **Regenerative Tracking** | Custom API integrations (e.g., carbon APIs) |
| **Testing** | Pytest, Mock (for APIs) |

* * *

# **Morbraii — business plan (revision 14, working)**

_(revision 13 → 14: the owner's new game_ **_Morbraii Mission — Acorn Tap_** _is built and verified by me in both modes, touch-first for phones; and the business name is corrected to_ **_Morbraii_** _everywhere it is shown — the one-i spelling was the typo.)_

## **What we're building**

Morbraii is **one message that any available channel can carry**. A letter or phrase is encoded once, then expressed through whichever channels the person still has: **timed vibration**, **light**, **tone**, or the **2×3 touch cell**. The codes are **Morse** (timed) and **Braille** (touch cells), bridged by a **visual hybrid glyph** that draws both at once, plus a **tactile-only font** for clean 1:1 interchange. The owner's goal: help people across **many situations** with **one definite communication solution that can transcend movement** — the code survives losing a channel (no vibration, no light, no hearing, no speech, no hand movement) instead of being tied to the one device you happen to hold. **Timing (owner): two profiles, both real.**

*   **Standard Morse (ITU)** — the true 1 : 3 : 1 : 3 : 7 unit grid at 5 / 8 / 12 wpm. What a learner acquires here reads on any real Morse channel.
    
*   **Morbraii spacing** — letters identical to standard (dot 1 unit, dash 3) with exaggerated boundaries (element 2 / letter 6 / word 14) so they can be felt, labelled on the site as ours and **not** ITU.
    

**Channels and representations (owner):**

*   **Tone — two live deliveries.** _Discrete pings_ ("on/off keying · standard") and a _sustained carrier_ ("ours · not ITU"): one tone that never goes silent, swelling while a dot or dash sounds and dipping in the gaps, so a boundary is heard as a drop in energy rather than silence. Same timing model and pitch map; waveform, register, per-user hearing ceiling and real Hz shown.
    
*   **Light** — the same rhythm with selectable colour sets.
    
*   **Vibration** — honest limit: the web Vibration API is on/off only. Frequency-tuned haptics need native access to the phone's actuator. We do not claim otherwise.
    
*   **Manual alphabet (live)** — A–Z **ASL one-handed fingerspelling** as SVG line art, beside the Morse wave, the Braille cell and the A–Z reference. Handshapes verified against cited references; **BSL is two-handed and is not shown**; **J and Z are motion letters** and the site says so; **nothing reads your hand**. Four drawing treatments exist (A default, B high-visibility, C filled silhouette, D print-intent) — the owner's pick is outstanding.
    
*   **Custom symbols (owner direction)** — draw your own character as vector paths, assign it the Morbraii switches. Not built.
    

**Games (owner direction) — one shell, many voices, and now a falling-acorn game.** A letter is already a rhythm and a pitch, so a piano, plucked, percussive or square-wave voice makes the same message playable without changing the code. Rules the team holds: no game gets its own timing or Hz table; synthesised voices are not sampled instruments and the copy says so; playable with mouse and keyboard alone, and now by touch alone; **no game claims to improve learning, retention, instrument skill or ASL recognition — none of that is measured**. **Games, built and verified.** The Games tab carries the piano, guitar and drum voices, an ear round, a **play-along lane**, free play, and **Morbraii Mission — Acorn Tap**.

*   **The play-along lane** judges on **when** you pressed (dead-on ±90 ms, early/late ±220 ms — our own hand-tuned windows, not measurements) and on the fret (number row 1–5, or clicking a fret button); every note is the letter's own Morse element at the shared unit and pitches. Start runs a visible **1800 ms count-in** and **nothing is scored during it** — verified: a press 461 ms into the count-in leaves the tally at all zeros with the judge still reading "No key pressed yet.", and a press on the first note is judged dead-on (measured at +8 and +3 ms on two runs, fret 1, A dot, A C5 520.0 Hz). The lane's missing lead-in — the defect I measured on 2026-10-20 — is fixed in 60 lane-scoped lines; no edit touches the Morse timing table, the unit grid, the Braille cell or the letters.
    
*   **Three voices on the one shell:** **Piano** (keys skin), **Guitar** (five strings, a fretboard band, a fret strip) and **Drum** (no skin). All three are one oscillator through the same gate — no samples, nothing recorded — and each keeps its own progress bucket (`morbrai.game.piano`, `.guitar`, `.drum`). Measured: the same two-note chart in all three voices gives **identical gates, 890 ms and 1770 ms** — the element length is the code and no voice shortens it.
    
*   **Acorn Tap (owner's request, 2026-10-27; built and verified by me).** Acorns fall down a chute carrying one letter's Morse; tap the matching answer to catch one. **Mode A · read the code** shows the dots and dashes and you tap the letter; **Mode B · know the code** shows the letter and you tap the pattern. Each acorn **sounds** its letter as it falls — the letter's own elements at the shared unit and the shared pitch map, in whichever voice is picked. Verified on the served page and in the export: mode A acorn `Morse .-` → tap "Answer A" → _caught · A is .- · streak 1_; a wrong tap → _wrong tap · W is not this acorn_ with the acorn still falling; mode B acorn `letter A` → tap `.-`; separate buckets `morbrai.game.acorn.read` and `.know`. It is the first game built **for a phone**: the game played by touch at a 390 × 844 viewport with every button measured (answers 177 × 64, mode buttons 270 × 56, start 330 × 56), no hover and no keyboard needed — and I widened one text link that was 16 px tall to a proper 48 px touch target.
    
*   **The ASL seam is in place, with no camera code:** every tap is judged by one function, so a hand-based input can be wired to the same check later. **The site's promise is unchanged** — "nothing on this page reads a camera, a microphone or your hand, no ASL recognition is built here".
    

**Frets on Fire steer (owner, 2026-10-19).** After playing _Frets on Fire_, the owner asked whether practising these communication styles might **incorporatively** teach a bit of guitar and piano. The guitar game is now a voice and a skin on the same lane, and the honest framing is written into the page itself: it practises rhythm, timing and pitch discrimination; it does **not** teach guitar, drums or piano (no strings, no fret positions, no chord shapes), the voices are oscillators and not sampled instruments, and "this also starts you on an instrument" is an unmeasured hypothesis that must never appear as a claim on the site. **ASL/camera branch — scouted, and the owner has now pointed at it.** The owner says Acorn Tap should also be made for **ASL hand recognition "when we have further development on camera ASL recognition"**. The assessment stands: build the **out** direction now (Morse → fingerspelling animation from the verified assets, labelled "fingerspelling, not ASL"); keep any camera work to a **measurement-only hand-landmark bench** (21 landmarks, is-a-hand, handedness, confidence, frame rate — **no classifier, no accuracy percentages**); and hold **full sign recognition** until there is an annotated corpus, a real phone and a Deaf signer's review. Before any camera code can ship the site's own promise has to be re-scoped — the wording I recommend is "no camera on this page; the landmark bench is a separate, clearly-labelled experiment". Written up at `/home/team/shared/asl-vision-branch-assessment.md`.

## **Who it's for**

Current hypothesis, in order of how close they are to us:

1.  **The owner as first learner** — the demo doubles as the teaching tool. If the owner cannot learn a letter by feel from it, nothing else matters.
    
2.  **People learning Morse by touch** rather than by ear.
    
3.  **People who lose a channel** (progressive sight or hearing loss, noisy or dark places, a phone that cannot vibrate) — the audience channel-independence is built for. The register control and hearing check exist because the pitch ladder climbs to G7 ≈ 3136 Hz, which age-related high-frequency loss can make inaudible — half the alphabet silent for exactly the people we are designing for.
    
4.  **Deafblind and low-vision-adjacent users** as the long-term audience; we have no evidence from them yet.
    

No user research exists. No deafblind or low-vision reviewer has seen this. No Deaf signer has reviewed the fingerspelling. Everything above is assumption, not data. **Adjacent ecosystem — Pierce (owner's steer, 2026-10-16).** The Pierce framework the owner is also building is _adapting and evolving, much like an ecosystem in and of itself_, so every read of it is a **dated snapshot**: re-read before quoting a figure, and depend on no single budget line — Morbraii's whole hardware requirement, one second-hand handset, is small enough to be carried by a device handover, a work-role budget, or an unrelated grant. Two unverified, uncommitted hypotheses: Pierce's accommodation spec has a _communication-access_ gap Morbraii's capability fits (written as the capability, not as "the Morbraii app", so the framework can adopt, replace or outgrow the tool); and Pierce residents are a possible first review population — with consent and an explicit no-outcome-claims rule. Nothing has been asked of them and no one there has seen this.

## **How it makes money**

**No money has moved. The business is on the cto.new free plan and its Stripe onboarding is not complete, so it cannot take a payment or send an invoice at all.** Completing Stripe onboarding on the Finance tab is what would make real transactions possible. The free plan has **hit its published-site limit**, so cto.new cannot publish the site. This no longer blocks us: the team produces a **static export** the owner can upload to any host he chooses, and it is verified to need no server-side code, no build step, no database and no external service. Publishing through cto.new still needs an upgrade on the billing page or archiving another business's site; uploading the export needs nothing from us. Untested candidates, hypotheses only: paid lesson packs or a full curriculum; licensing the bridging and tactile-only fonts; a teaching tool for schools. None has been priced, offered or tested, and there is nothing for sale on the site.

## **Current focus**

Ship a phone-friendly web demo that proves the body can learn the code, then make it work on **every** phone and in **every** channel — and make it reachable without depending on cto.new's publish limit. **Shippable now — the static export (regenerated 2026-10-27, verified by me).** `/home/team/shared/hosting/morbrai-site-2026-10-27.zip`, **1.64 MB**, extracting to 17 files, regenerated by one command (`bash /home/team/shared/hosting/work/export.sh`) and documented in the `DEPLOY.md` inside it. Verified served from a plain static file server (no app server involved): `/`, `/framework/`, `/receive-lab.html`, `/receive-summary.json`, all four CSS/JS bundles and the test clips each answered **200**; the page hydrated in a real browser with all **seven** tabs switching; the guard rails were unchanged (`dot 240 ms · ▬ dash 720 ms · 240 ms gaps · letter gap 720 ms · word gap 1680 ms`; `buzz pattern: [240, 240, 720] ms`); and in the uploaded copy the Acorn Tap game caught a letter in mode A (`Answer A` → caught, streak 1, bucket `morbrai.game.acorn.read`) and the lane scored dead-on on its first note. The title now reads **Morbraii — Touch is a language**. The export carries `404.html`, `_redirects` and `.nojekyll` fallbacks, and its asset links are root-absolute — so it needs a **domain root or subdomain root**, not a subfolder of someone else's site. The owner has not named a host; when he does the export is adapted if needed. **Live and verified on the working site:** letter picker A–Z; hybrid glyph (Morse wave + Braille cell) with a large tactile-only Braille view and the manual alphabet beside it; word melody with paragraph input (240-character cap stated in the UI, spaces as real word gaps); **Lessons 1–5** ending in the flagship **"MIRACLES HAPPEN EVERY SECOND"** phrase; Lesson 4 line stacking; full A–Z reference plus the 26-sign ASL grid; **light mode** with three colour sets; **both timing profiles**; **tone reach rounds 1 and 2**; the **listening prototype** with both its honesty fixes; the **tabbed layout** (Letters / Melody / Lessons / Games / A–Z & signs / Setup / Classic) with the old long scroll kept as "Classic"; and the **Games tab** with its lane, its three voices and Acorn Tap. **Owner review package — delivered 2026-10-19, now superseded as a snapshot.** Three single-file offline pages plus a guide and a one-page state summary, zipped flat at `/home/team/shared/review-package/morbrai-review-2026-10-19.zip` (~1.9 MB), verified to make **zero network requests** in offline mode. It **predates** the listening fixes, the games build, the lane fix and Acorn Tap — the export above is the up-to-date copy. **Standing discipline:** every claim about timing or a code value is backed by a measurement on the live page or a fetched reference — never by memory or by reading our own code. This includes our own errors: on 2026-10-17 a tone alarm was raised and withdrawn because the probe sorted audio taps by loudness and picked a constant pre-envelope gain node (RMS 0.5196 = 0.9/√3) instead of the keyed envelope; the engine had been keying correctly all along. The trap is in the team's measurement skill. **Tone, measured 2026-10-17 (Standard 5 wpm, AudioContext running):** letter A produces **two separate sound envelopes, attacks 484 ms apart** against a 480 ms nominal — one envelope per element. Carrier mode over "A B": dot 250 · element gap 225 · dash 725 · **word gap 1675** (nominal 1680) · dot-to-dot 475 (nominal 480). The live acceptance values — letter gap ≈730 ms and word gap ≈1680 ms — hold. **Which surfaces key:** `📳 Feel it: {letter}`, the lessons, the quiz target, the **melody in carrier mode**, the **games' lane, round and acorns** key Morse — one envelope per element. The tone panel's `▶ Hear {letter} at {Hz} Hz` is a **pitch note** that auditions the plan, and the **melody in discrete mode plays one note per letter** by design. **The receive path — the sweep is finished, and its one unmeasured case is now measured.** Microphone → RMS envelope → noise floor tracked from the signal → element durations → inferred unit → letters. Of 20 laboratory cases: **19 ran, 17 produced letters, 2 refused honestly, 1 is inconclusive, none unrun**; **48 of 59 letters correct**, **12 of 19 whole messages exact**, highest confidence 60%. Two elements now decodes — at a **2500 ms** flush window the same recording gives `E T` in one message, unit inferred 239.6 ms against a true 240 (−0.2%), confidence **36%**, printed **tentative**. The page states plainly that confidence is a **fit-error readout, not a probability of being right**, and that its highest value (60%, exactly the page's own bar) went to a wrong decode. **Still failing, stated plainly:** 8 wpm — the middle of the site's three learning speeds — produced no letter on a clean, loud synthetic case; noise does not degrade gradually; reverb decoded wrong; a single element is refused honestly. **Honest bounds:** every row is a **synthetic WAV**, with no phone, no room and no real buzzer ever involved, and the microphone path's use of the new flush window is a **code-path claim with no live measurement** (headless Chromium here exposes no capture device). **Two decisions the owner owns (product calls, not bugs):**

1.  The control reads "Discrete pings · on/off keying", but the melody in that mode plays **one note per letter**. Either the copy says "a note per letter", or the melody keys in discrete mode.
    
2.  In discrete mode, gaps between elements are **audible re-strikes rather than true silence** (the dot's tail is still −24 dB at the end of the gap); letter and word gaps do reach silence. If "on/off keying" is the promise, a shorter decay is the lever.
    

**In build, in order:**

1.  **Games** — the shell, three voices and Acorn Tap are built and verified. Next: the **8-bit voice** the shell was designed to take, then the **retention-game concept**, which is agreed with the owner before any build — four questions outstanding, none answered (daily set or open-ended; test sending as well as reading; a reason to return that is not a score; where the flagship phrase sits).
    
2.  **ASL phrase set** — useful words shown fingerspelled letter by letter, plus the **Morse → fingerspelling animation** (the "out" direction). Honest limit: fingerspelling is not ASL grammar, and we will not invent signs.
    
3.  **Refreshed offline review package**, regenerated from the current site. Still queued.
    
4.  **Voice dictation as an input channel** — assessment first: browser support, the privacy cost of server-side recognition, iOS reality, and what it changes for someone who cannot speak.
    
5.  **Queued small items** — the melody box swallows typing while it plays (to be established as a defect or a deliberate choice, then measured); the Lesson 4 line-to-line Play-all gap has never been measured; the pages log React hydration-mismatch warnings on load that predate the games build (measured: games activity adds none).
    

## **KPIs**

**No analytics and no measured usage of any kind** — no visitors, sessions or completion rates. Anything numeric today is a target, not a result. Real, measured: the working site serves all five lessons, the phrase player, light mode, both timing profiles, both tone deliveries, the full ASL alphabet in four drawing treatments, the listening prototype, the tabbed layout with Classic preserved, and a Games tab with a count-in lane, **three synthesised voices sharing one chart and one judge**, and **Acorn Tap playable in two modes by touch at a phone viewport**; four sensory channels exist per letter (vibration, tone, light, Braille cell) plus two visual representations (glyph, manual alphabet); the Standard profile's element, letter and word gaps measure at the correct 1, 3 and 7 unit values; the receive sweep is complete at 48/59 letters with 12/19 exact messages, 2 honest refusals and 1 inconclusive case; the offline review package was delivered and verified to make zero network requests; and the **static export** is delivered — 1.64 MB, 17 files, every route and asset serving 200 from a plain static file server, all seven tabs hydrating, guard rails intact, no `localhost` baked in, title corrected to Morbraii. Runs that have _not_ produced a number: **0** human testers, **0** devices other than a desktop browser, **0** phone vibration tests, **0** human game sessions. The first signal worth chasing is still not a web metric: **can the owner feel a phrase and read letters off it without looking — and does that hold at standard Morse spacing?** No user has ever tried this, including the owner, and he has no working handset at present, so it has not run. Its tone and light halves can be run on a computer meanwhile — and the export means he can run them from his own hosting on any phone he picks up; the vibration half waits for a phone.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>256 Spheres Grid (Three.js)</title>
  <style>
    body { margin: 0; overflow: hidden; }
    canvas { display: block; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <script src="[https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.132.2/build/three.min.js"></script>](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.132.2/build/three.min.js"></script>)
  <script src="[https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.132.2/examples/js/controls/OrbitControls.js"></script>](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.132.2/examples/js/controls/OrbitControls.js"></script>)
  <script>
    // Scene setup
    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(75, window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight, 0.1, 1000);
    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas: document.body.appendChild(document.createElement('canvas')) });
    renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight);
    document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
    // Controls for camera movement
    const controls = new THREE.OrbitControls(camera, renderer.domElement);
    camera.position.z = 20;
    // Create 256 spheres in a 16x16 grid
    const gridSize = 16; // 16x16 = 256
    const sphereRadius = 0.5;
    const spacing = 3.0; // Distance between spheres
    for (let row = 0; row < gridSize; row++) {
      for (let col = 0; col < gridSize; col++) {
        // Calculate position (x, y, z)
        const x = (col - gridSize / 2) * spacing;
        const y = (row - gridSize / 2) * spacing;
        const z = 0;
        // Create a sphere
        const geometry = new THREE.SphereGeometry(sphereRadius, 32, 32);
        const material = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({
          color: Math.random() * 0xffffff, // Random color
          roughness: 0.3,
          metalness: 0.5
        });
        const sphere = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
        sphere.position.set(x, y, z);
        scene.add(sphere);
      }
    }
    // Add lights
    const ambientLight = new THREE.AmbientLight(0xffffff, 0.5);
    scene.add(ambientLight);
    const directionalLight = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 0.8);
    directionalLight.position.set(10, 10, 5);
    scene.add(directionalLight);
    // Animation loop
    function animate() {
      requestAnimationFrame(animate);
      controls.update();
      renderer.render(scene, camera);
    }
    animate();
    // Handle window resize
    window.addEventListener('resize', () => {
      camera.aspect = window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight;
      camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
      renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight);
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>

To build a **Payroll Python Application** for your **Universal Regenerative Universal Basic Income (RUHBI)** concept, we’ll need a structured approach that integrates financial processing, user management, and regenerative economic principles. Below is a **step-by-step breakdown** of how we can design this system, including key components, Python libraries, and automation workflows.

* * *

### **1. Core Features of the RUHBI Payroll System**

Your **RUHBI** concept likely involves:

*   **Universal Basic Income (UBI) distribution** (periodic, unconditional payments).
    
*   **Regenerative economic incentives** (e.g., rewards for sustainable/regenerative activities).
    
*   **Transparent financial tracking** (blockchain-like ledger for trust).
    
*   **Automated compliance** (taxes, social contributions, environmental impact reporting).
    
*   **User self-service portal** (claims, payouts, impact tracking).

We’ll use:

*   **Backend**: Python (Flask/FastAPI) for REST APIs.
    
*   **Database**: PostgreSQL (for relational data) + optional IPFS/Blockchain (for transparency).
    
*   **Automation**: Scheduled tasks (Celery) for payouts/tax deductions.
    
*   **Frontend**: Optional (React/Dash for dashboards) or CLI/API-based.

Let’s Go into regenerative scoring and also include an integrative concept as well that is in developement:

# **Morbraii — business plan (revision 14, working)**

_(revision 13 → 14: the owner's new game_ **_Morbraii Mission — Acorn Tap_** _is built and verified by me in both modes, touch-first for phones; and the business name is corrected to_ **_Morbraii_** _everywhere it is shown — the one-i spelling was the typo.)_

## **What we're building**

Morbraii is **one message that any available channel can carry**. A letter or phrase is encoded once, then expressed through whichever channels the person still has: **timed vibration**, **light**, **tone**, or the **2×3 touch cell**. The codes are **Morse** (timed) and **Braille** (touch cells), bridged by a **visual hybrid glyph** that draws both at once, plus a **tactile-only font** for clean 1:1 interchange. The owner's goal: help people across **many situations** with **one definite communication solution that can transcend movement** — the code survives losing a channel (no vibration, no light, no hearing, no speech, no hand movement) instead of being tied to the one device you happen to hold. **Timing (owner): two profiles, both real.**

*   **Standard Morse (ITU)** — the true 1 : 3 : 1 : 3 : 7 unit grid at 5 / 8 / 12 wpm. What a learner acquires here reads on any real Morse channel.
    
*   **Morbraii spacing** — letters identical to standard (dot 1 unit, dash 3) with exaggerated boundaries (element 2 / letter 6 / word 14) so they can be felt, labelled on the site as ours and **not** ITU.
    

**Channels and representations (owner):**

*   **Tone — two live deliveries.** _Discrete pings_ ("on/off keying · standard") and a _sustained carrier_ ("ours · not ITU"): one tone that never goes silent, swelling while a dot or dash sounds and dipping in the gaps, so a boundary is heard as a drop in energy rather than silence. Same timing model and pitch map; waveform, register, per-user hearing ceiling and real Hz shown.
    
*   **Light** — the same rhythm with selectable colour sets.
    
*   **Vibration** — honest limit: the web Vibration API is on/off only. Frequency-tuned haptics need native access to the phone's actuator. We do not claim otherwise.
    
*   **Manual alphabet (live)** — A–Z **ASL one-handed fingerspelling** as SVG line art, beside the Morse wave, the Braille cell and the A–Z reference. Handshapes verified against cited references; **BSL is two-handed and is not shown**; **J and Z are motion letters** and the site says so; **nothing reads your hand**. Four drawing treatments exist (A default, B high-visibility, C filled silhouette, D print-intent) — the owner's pick is outstanding.
    
*   **Custom symbols (owner direction)** — draw your own character as vector paths, assign it the Morbraii switches. Not built.
    

**Games (owner direction) — one shell, many voices, and now a falling-acorn game.** A letter is already a rhythm and a pitch, so a piano, plucked, percussive or square-wave voice makes the same message playable without changing the code. Rules the team holds: no game gets its own timing or Hz table; synthesised voices are not sampled instruments and the copy says so; playable with mouse and keyboard alone, and now by touch alone; **no game claims to improve learning, retention, instrument skill or ASL recognition — none of that is measured**. **Games, built and verified.** The Games tab carries the piano, guitar and drum voices, an ear round, a **play-along lane**, free play, and **Morbraii Mission — Acorn Tap**.

*   **The play-along lane** judges on **when** you pressed (dead-on ±90 ms, early/late ±220 ms — our own hand-tuned windows, not measurements) and on the fret (number row 1–5, or clicking a fret button); every note is the letter's own Morse element at the shared unit and pitches. Start runs a visible **1800 ms count-in** and **nothing is scored during it** — verified: a press 461 ms into the count-in leaves the tally at all zeros with the judge still reading "No key pressed yet.", and a press on the first note is judged dead-on (measured at +8 and +3 ms on two runs, fret 1, A dot, A C5 520.0 Hz). The lane's missing lead-in — the defect I measured on 2026-10-20 — is fixed in 60 lane-scoped lines; no edit touches the Morse timing table, the unit grid, the Braille cell or the letters.
    
*   **Three voices on the one shell:** **Piano** (keys skin), **Guitar** (five strings, a fretboard band, a fret strip) and **Drum** (no skin). All three are one oscillator through the same gate — no samples, nothing recorded — and each keeps its own progress bucket (`morbrai.game.piano`, `.guitar`, `.drum`). Measured: the same two-note chart in all three voices gives **identical gates, 890 ms and 1770 ms** — the element length is the code and no voice shortens it.
    
*   **Acorn Tap (owner's request, 2026-10-27; built and verified by me).** Acorns fall down a chute carrying one letter's Morse; tap the matching answer to catch one. **Mode A · read the code** shows the dots and dashes and you tap the letter; **Mode B · know the code** shows the letter and you tap the pattern. Each acorn **sounds** its letter as it falls — the letter's own elements at the shared unit and the shared pitch map, in whichever voice is picked. Verified on the served page and in the export: mode A acorn `Morse .-` → tap "Answer A" → _caught · A is .- · streak 1_; a wrong tap → _wrong tap · W is not this acorn_ with the acorn still falling; mode B acorn `letter A` → tap `.-`; separate buckets `morbrai.game.acorn.read` and `.know`. It is the first game built **for a phone**: the game played by touch at a 390 × 844 viewport with every button measured (answers 177 × 64, mode buttons 270 × 56, start 330 × 56), no hover and no keyboard needed — and I widened one text link that was 16 px tall to a proper 48 px touch target.
    
*   **The ASL seam is in place, with no camera code:** every tap is judged by one function, so a hand-based input can be wired to the same check later. **The site's promise is unchanged** — "nothing on this page reads a camera, a microphone or your hand, no ASL recognition is built here".
    

**Frets on Fire steer (owner, 2026-10-19).** After playing _Frets on Fire_, the owner asked whether practising these communication styles might **incorporatively** teach a bit of guitar and piano. The guitar game is now a voice and a skin on the same lane, and the honest framing is written into the page itself: it practises rhythm, timing and pitch discrimination; it does **not** teach guitar, drums or piano (no strings, no fret positions, no chord shapes), the voices are oscillators and not sampled instruments, and "this also starts you on an instrument" is an unmeasured hypothesis that must never appear as a claim on the site. **ASL/camera branch — scouted, and the owner has now pointed at it.** The owner says Acorn Tap should also be made for **ASL hand recognition "when we have further development on camera ASL recognition"**. The assessment stands: build the **out** direction now (Morse → fingerspelling animation from the verified assets, labelled "fingerspelling, not ASL"); keep any camera work to a **measurement-only hand-landmark bench** (21 landmarks, is-a-hand, handedness, confidence, frame rate — **no classifier, no accuracy percentages**); and hold **full sign recognition** until there is an annotated corpus, a real phone and a Deaf signer's review. Before any camera code can ship the site's own promise has to be re-scoped — the wording I recommend is "no camera on this page; the landmark bench is a separate, clearly-labelled experiment". Written up at `/home/team/shared/asl-vision-branch-assessment.md`.

## **Who it's for**

Current hypothesis, in order of how close they are to us:

1.  **The owner as first learner** — the demo doubles as the teaching tool. If the owner cannot learn a letter by feel from it, nothing else matters.
    
2.  **People learning Morse by touch** rather than by ear.
    
3.  **People who lose a channel** (progressive sight or hearing loss, noisy or dark places, a phone that cannot vibrate) — the audience channel-independence is built for. The register control and hearing check exist because the pitch ladder climbs to G7 ≈ 3136 Hz, which age-related high-frequency loss can make inaudible — half the alphabet silent for exactly the people we are designing for.
    
4.  **Deafblind and low-vision-adjacent users** as the long-term audience; we have no evidence from them yet.
    

No user research exists. No deafblind or low-vision reviewer has seen this. No Deaf signer has reviewed the fingerspelling. Everything above is assumption, not data. **Adjacent ecosystem — Pierce (owner's steer, 2026-10-16).** The Pierce framework the owner is also building is _adapting and evolving, much like an ecosystem in and of itself_, so every read of it is a **dated snapshot**: re-read before quoting a figure, and depend on no single budget line — Morbraii's whole hardware requirement, one second-hand handset, is small enough to be carried by a device handover, a work-role budget, or an unrelated grant. Two unverified, uncommitted hypotheses: Pierce's accommodation spec has a _communication-access_ gap Morbraii's capability fits (written as the capability, not as "the Morbraii app", so the framework can adopt, replace or outgrow the tool); and Pierce residents are a possible first review population — with consent and an explicit no-outcome-claims rule. Nothing has been asked of them and no one there has seen this.

## **How it makes money**

**No money has moved. The business is on the cto.new free plan and its Stripe onboarding is not complete, so it cannot take a payment or send an invoice at all.** Completing Stripe onboarding on the Finance tab is what would make real transactions possible. The free plan has **hit its published-site limit**, so cto.new cannot publish the site. This no longer blocks us: the team produces a **static export** the owner can upload to any host he chooses, and it is verified to need no server-side code, no build step, no database and no external service. Publishing through cto.new still needs an upgrade on the billing page or archiving another business's site; uploading the export needs nothing from us. Untested candidates, hypotheses only: paid lesson packs or a full curriculum; licensing the bridging and tactile-only fonts; a teaching tool for schools. None has been priced, offered or tested, and there is nothing for sale on the site.

## **Current focus**

Ship a phone-friendly web demo that proves the body can learn the code, then make it work on **every** phone and in **every** channel — and make it reachable without depending on cto.new's publish limit. **Shippable now — the static export (regenerated 2026-10-27, verified by me).** `/home/team/shared/hosting/morbrai-site-2026-10-27.zip`, **1.64 MB**, extracting to 17 files, regenerated by one command (`bash /home/team/shared/hosting/work/export.sh`) and documented in the `DEPLOY.md` inside it. Verified served from a plain static file server (no app server involved): `/`, `/framework/`, `/receive-lab.html`, `/receive-summary.json`, all four CSS/JS bundles and the test clips each answered **200**; the page hydrated in a real browser with all **seven** tabs switching; the guard rails were unchanged (`dot 240 ms · ▬ dash 720 ms · 240 ms gaps · letter gap 720 ms · word gap 1680 ms`; `buzz pattern: [240, 240, 720] ms`); and in the uploaded copy the Acorn Tap game caught a letter in mode A (`Answer A` → caught, streak 1, bucket `morbrai.game.acorn.read`) and the lane scored dead-on on its first note. The title now reads **Morbraii — Touch is a language**. The export carries `404.html`, `_redirects` and `.nojekyll` fallbacks, and its asset links are root-absolute — so it needs a **domain root or subdomain root**, not a subfolder of someone else's site. The owner has not named a host; when he does the export is adapted if needed. **Live and verified on the working site:** letter picker A–Z; hybrid glyph (Morse wave + Braille cell) with a large tactile-only Braille view and the manual alphabet beside it; word melody with paragraph input (240-character cap stated in the UI, spaces as real word gaps); **Lessons 1–5** ending in the flagship **"MIRACLES HAPPEN EVERY SECOND"** phrase; Lesson 4 line stacking; full A–Z reference plus the 26-sign ASL grid; **light mode** with three colour sets; **both timing profiles**; **tone reach rounds 1 and 2**; the **listening prototype** with both its honesty fixes; the **tabbed layout** (Letters / Melody / Lessons / Games / A–Z & signs / Setup / Classic) with the old long scroll kept as "Classic"; and the **Games tab** with its lane, its three voices and Acorn Tap. **Owner review package — delivered 2026-10-19, now superseded as a snapshot.** Three single-file offline pages plus a guide and a one-page state summary, zipped flat at `/home/team/shared/review-package/morbrai-review-2026-10-19.zip` (~1.9 MB), verified to make **zero network requests** in offline mode. It **predates** the listening fixes, the games build, the lane fix and Acorn Tap — the export above is the up-to-date copy. **Standing discipline:** every claim about timing or a code value is backed by a measurement on the live page or a fetched reference — never by memory or by reading our own code. This includes our own errors: on 2026-10-17 a tone alarm was raised and withdrawn because the probe sorted audio taps by loudness and picked a constant pre-envelope gain node (RMS 0.5196 = 0.9/√3) instead of the keyed envelope; the engine had been keying correctly all along. The trap is in the team's measurement skill. **Tone, measured 2026-10-17 (Standard 5 wpm, AudioContext running):** letter A produces **two separate sound envelopes, attacks 484 ms apart** against a 480 ms nominal — one envelope per element. Carrier mode over "A B": dot 250 · element gap 225 · dash 725 · **word gap 1675** (nominal 1680) · dot-to-dot 475 (nominal 480). The live acceptance values — letter gap ≈730 ms and word gap ≈1680 ms — hold. **Which surfaces key:** `📳 Feel it: {letter}`, the lessons, the quiz target, the **melody in carrier mode**, the **games' lane, round and acorns** key Morse — one envelope per element. The tone panel's `▶ Hear {letter} at {Hz} Hz` is a **pitch note** that auditions the plan, and the **melody in discrete mode plays one note per letter** by design. **The receive path — the sweep is finished, and its one unmeasured case is now measured.** Microphone → RMS envelope → noise floor tracked from the signal → element durations → inferred unit → letters. Of 20 laboratory cases: **19 ran, 17 produced letters, 2 refused honestly, 1 is inconclusive, none unrun**; **48 of 59 letters correct**, **12 of 19 whole messages exact**, highest confidence 60%. Two elements now decodes — at a **2500 ms** flush window the same recording gives `E T` in one message, unit inferred 239.6 ms against a true 240 (−0.2%), confidence **36%**, printed **tentative**. The page states plainly that confidence is a **fit-error readout, not a probability of being right**, and that its highest value (60%, exactly the page's own bar) went to a wrong decode. **Still failing, stated plainly:** 8 wpm — the middle of the site's three learning speeds — produced no letter on a clean, loud synthetic case; noise does not degrade gradually; reverb decoded wrong; a single element is refused honestly. **Honest bounds:** every row is a **synthetic WAV**, with no phone, no room and no real buzzer ever involved, and the microphone path's use of the new flush window is a **code-path claim with no live measurement** (headless Chromium here exposes no capture device). **Two decisions the owner owns (product calls, not bugs):**

1.  The control reads "Discrete pings · on/off keying", but the melody in that mode plays **one note per letter**. Either the copy says "a note per letter", or the melody keys in discrete mode.
    
2.  In discrete mode, gaps between elements are **audible re-strikes rather than true silence** (the dot's tail is still −24 dB at the end of the gap); letter and word gaps do reach silence. If "on/off keying" is the promise, a shorter decay is the lever.
    

**In build, in order:**

1.  **Games** — the shell, three voices and Acorn Tap are built and verified. Next: the **8-bit voice** the shell was designed to take, then the **retention-game concept**, which is agreed with the owner before any build — four questions outstanding, none answered (daily set or open-ended; test sending as well as reading; a reason to return that is not a score; where the flagship phrase sits).
    
2.  **ASL phrase set** — useful words shown fingerspelled letter by letter, plus the **Morse → fingerspelling animation** (the "out" direction). Honest limit: fingerspelling is not ASL grammar, and we will not invent signs.
    
3.  **Refreshed offline review package**, regenerated from the current site. Still queued.
    
4.  **Voice dictation as an input channel** — assessment first: browser support, the privacy cost of server-side recognition, iOS reality, and what it changes for someone who cannot speak.
    
5.  **Queued small items** — the melody box swallows typing while it plays (to be established as a defect or a deliberate choice, then measured); the Lesson 4 line-to-line Play-all gap has never been measured; the pages log React hydration-mismatch warnings on load that predate the games build (measured: games activity adds none).
    

## **KPIs**

**No analytics and no measured usage of any kind** — no visitors, sessions or completion rates. Anything numeric today is a target, not a result. Real, measured: the working site serves all five lessons, the phrase player, light mode, both timing profiles, both tone deliveries, the full ASL alphabet in four drawing treatments, the listening prototype, the tabbed layout with Classic preserved, and a Games tab with a count-in lane, **three synthesised voices sharing one chart and one judge**, and **Acorn Tap playable in two modes by touch at a phone viewport**; four sensory channels exist per letter (vibration, tone, light, Braille cell) plus two visual representations (glyph, manual alphabet); the Standard profile's element, letter and word gaps measure at the correct 1, 3 and 7 unit values; the receive sweep is complete at 48/59 letters with 12/19 exact messages, 2 honest refusals and 1 inconclusive case; the offline review package was delivered and verified to make zero network requests; and the **static export** is delivered — 1.64 MB, 17 files, every route and asset serving 200 from a plain static file server, all seven tabs hydrating, guard rails intact, no `localhost` baked in, title corrected to Morbraii. Runs that have _not_ produced a number: **0** human testers, **0** devices other than a desktop browser, **0** phone vibration tests, **0** human game sessions. <html>
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>256 Spheres Grid (Three.js)</title>
  <style>
    body { margin: 0; overflow: hidden; }
    canvas { display: block; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <script src="[https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.132.2/build/three.min.js"></script>](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.132.2/build/three.min.js"></script>)
  <script src="[https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.132.2/examples/js/controls/OrbitControls.js"></script>](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.132.2/examples/js/controls/OrbitControls.js"></script>)
  <script>
    // Scene setup
    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(75, window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight, 0.1, 1000);
    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas: document.body.appendChild(document.createElement('canvas')) });
    renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight);
    document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
    // Controls for camera movement
    const controls = new THREE.OrbitControls(camera, renderer.domElement);
    camera.position.z = 20;
    // Create 256 spheres in a 16x16 grid
    const gridSize = 16; // 16x16 = 256
    const sphereRadius = 0.5;
    const spacing = 3.0; // Distance between spheres
    for (let row = 0; row < gridSize; row++) {
      for (let col = 0; col < gridSize; col++) {
        // Calculate position (x, y, z)
        const x = (col - gridSize / 2) * spacing;
        const y = (row - gridSize / 2) * spacing;
        const z = 0;
        // Create a sphere
        const geometry = new THREE.SphereGeometry(sphereRadius, 32, 32);
        const material = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({
          color: Math.random() * 0xffffff, // Random color
          roughness: 0.3,
          metalness: 0.5
        });
        const sphere = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
        sphere.position.set(x, y, z);
        scene.add(sphere);
      }
    }
    // Add lights
    const ambientLight = new THREE.AmbientLight(0xffffff, 0.5);
    scene.add(ambientLight);
    const directionalLight = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 0.8);
    directionalLight.position.set(10, 10, 5);
    scene.add(directionalLight);
    // Animation loop
    function animate() {
      requestAnimationFrame(animate);
      controls.update();
      renderer.render(scene, camera);
    }
    animate();
    // Handle window resize
    window.addEventListener('resize', () => {
      camera.aspect = window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight;
      camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
      renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight);
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>

## **What we're building**

Morbraii is **one message that any available channel can carry**. A letter or phrase is encoded once, then expressed through whichever channels the person still has: **timed vibration**, **light**, **tone**, or the **2×3 touch cell**. The codes are **Morse** (timed) and **Braille** (touch cells), bridged by a **visual hybrid glyph** that draws both at once, plus a **tactile-only font** for clean 1:1 interchange. The owner's goal: help people across **many situations** with **one definite communication solution that can transcend movement** — the code survives losing a channel (no vibration, no light, no hearing, no speech, no hand movement) instead of being tied to the one device you happen to hold. **Timing (owner): two profiles, both real.**

*   **Standard Morse (ITU)** — the true 1 : 3 : 1 : 3 : 7 unit grid at 5 / 8 / 12 wpm. What a learner acquires here reads on any real Morse channel.
    
*   **Morbraii spacing** — letters identical to standard (dot 1 unit, dash 3) with exaggerated boundaries (element 2 / letter 6 / word 14) so they can be felt, labelled on the site as ours and **not** ITU.
    

**Channels and representations (owner):**

*   **Tone — two live deliveries.** _Discrete pings_ ("on/off keying · standard") and a _sustained carrier_ ("ours · not ITU"): one tone that never goes silent, swelling while a dot or dash sounds and dipping in the gaps, so a boundary is heard as a drop in energy rather than silence. Same timing model and pitch map; waveform, register, per-user hearing ceiling and real Hz shown.
    
*   **Light** — the same rhythm with selectable colour sets.
    
*   **Vibration** — honest limit: the web Vibration API is on/off only. Frequency-tuned haptics need native access to the phone's actuator. We do not claim otherwise.
    
*   **Manual alphabet (live)** — A–Z **ASL one-handed fingerspelling** as SVG line art, beside the Morse wave, the Braille cell and the A–Z reference. Handshapes verified against cited references; **BSL is two-handed and is not shown**; **J and Z are motion letters** and the site says so; **nothing reads your hand**. Four drawing treatments exist (A default, B high-visibility, C filled silhouette, D print-intent) — the owner's pick is outstanding.
    
*   **Custom symbols (owner direction)** — draw your own character as vector paths, assign it the Morbraii switches. Not built.
    

**Games (owner direction) — one shell, many voices, and now a falling-acorn game.** A letter is already a rhythm and a pitch, so a piano, plucked, percussive or square-wave voice makes the same message playable without changing the code. Rules the team holds: no game gets its own timing or Hz table; synthesised voices are not sampled instruments and the copy says so; playable with mouse and keyboard alone, and now by touch alone; **no game claims to improve learning, retention, instrument skill or ASL recognition — none of that is measured**. **Games, built and verified.** The Games tab carries the piano, guitar and drum voices, an ear round, a **play-along lane**, free play, and **Morbraii Mission — Acorn Tap**.

*   **The play-along lane** judges on **when** you pressed (dead-on ±90 ms, early/late ±220 ms — our own hand-tuned windows, not measurements) and on the fret (number row 1–5, or clicking a fret button); every note is the letter's own Morse element at the shared unit and pitches. Start runs a visible **1800 ms count-in** and **nothing is scored during it** — verified: a press 461 ms into the count-in leaves the tally at all zeros with the judge still reading "No key pressed yet.", and a press on the first note is judged dead-on (measured at +8 and +3 ms on two runs, fret 1, A dot, A C5 520.0 Hz). The lane's missing lead-in — the defect I measured on 2026-10-20 — is fixed in 60 lane-scoped lines; no edit touches the Morse timing table, the unit grid, the Braille cell or the letters.
    
*   **Three voices on the one shell:** **Piano** (keys skin), **Guitar** (five strings, a fretboard band, a fret strip) and **Drum** (no skin). All three are one oscillator through the same gate — no samples, nothing recorded — and each keeps its own progress bucket (`morbrai.game.piano`, `.guitar`, `.drum`). Measured: the same two-note chart in all three voices gives **identical gates, 890 ms and 1770 ms** — the element length is the code and no voice shortens it.
    
*   **Acorn Tap (owner's request, 2026-10-27; built and verified by me).** Acorns fall down a chute carrying one letter's Morse; tap the matching answer to catch one. **Mode A · read the code** shows the dots and dashes and you tap the letter; **Mode B · know the code** shows the letter and you tap the pattern. Each acorn **sounds** its letter as it falls — the letter's own elements at the shared unit and the shared pitch map, in whichever voice is picked. Verified on the served page and in the export: mode A acorn `Morse .-` → tap "Answer A" → _caught · A is .- · streak 1_; a wrong tap → _wrong tap · W is not this acorn_ with the acorn still falling; mode B acorn `letter A` → tap `.-`; separate buckets `morbrai.game.acorn.read` and `.know`. It is the first game built **for a phone**: the game played by touch at a 390 × 844 viewport with every button measured (answers 177 × 64, mode buttons 270 × 56, start 330 × 56), no hover and no keyboard needed — and I widened one text link that was 16 px tall to a proper 48 px touch target.
    
*   **The ASL seam is in place, with no camera code:** every tap is judged by one function, so a hand-based input can be wired to the same check later. **The site's promise is unchanged** — "nothing on this page reads a camera, a microphone or your hand, no ASL recognition is built here".
    

**Frets on Fire steer (owner, 2026-10-19).** After playing _Frets on Fire_, the owner asked whether practising these communication styles might **incorporatively** teach a bit of guitar and piano.   <script>
    // Scene setup
    const scene = new THREE.Scene();
    const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(75, window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight, 0.1, 1000);
    const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas: document.body.appendChild(document.createElement('canvas')) });
    renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight);
    document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
    // Controls for camera movement
    const controls = new THREE.OrbitControls(camera, renderer.domElement);
    camera.position.z = 20;
    // Create 256 spheres in a 16x16 grid
    const gridSize = 16; // 16x16 = 256
    const sphereRadius = 0.5;
    const spacing = 3.0; // Distance between spheres
    for (let row = 0; row < gridSize; row++) {
      for (let col = 0; col < gridSize; col++) {
        // Calculate position (x, y, z)
        const x = (col - gridSize / 2) * spacing;
        const y = (row - gridSize / 2) * spacing;
        const z = 0;
        // Create a sphere
        const geometry = new THREE.SphereGeometry(sphereRadius, 32, 32);
        const material = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({
          color: Math.random() * 0xffffff, // Random color
          roughness: 0.3,
          metalness: 0.5
        });
        const sphere = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
        sphere.position.set(x, y, z);
        scene.add(sphere);
      }
    }
    // Add lights
    const ambientLight = new THREE.AmbientLight(0xffffff, 0.5);
    scene.add(ambientLight);
    const directionalLight = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 0.8);
    directionalLight.position.set(10, 10, 5);
    scene.add(directionalLight);
    // Animation loop
    function animate() {
      requestAnimationFrame(animate);
      controls.update();
      renderer.render(scene, camera);
    }
    animate();
    // Handle window resize
    window.addEventListener('resize', () => {
      camera.aspect = window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight;
      camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
      renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight);
    });
  </script>
</body>
